Terah
tē'rä
n. (father of Abram, Nahor and Haran; an idolater out of Ur who began the journey to Canaan and stopped short of it)
From Hebrew Terach, of uncertain derivation. Luke's genealogy renders the name Thara. The man is remembered less for what the name means than for where he stopped.

Biblical Definition

Terah is the father of Abram, and Joshua tells Israel plainly what he was: “Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods” (Jos 24:2). The line of promise begins in a house of idols. That is the first thing to say about Terah, and it is the reason Abram's call is called grace and not merit. The second thing is stranger. Terah himself set out: “Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law… and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan” (Gen 11:31). The destination is named. He intended Canaan. And the verse ends: “they came unto Haran, and dwelt there”. He got halfway, found a place that suited him, and settled. “The days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran” (Gen 11:32). Only after his death does God's word come again and Abram go on. Terah is the man who left Ur and never reached Canaan — not because the road closed, but because Haran was comfortable. Scripture never says he sinned in stopping. It simply records that he stopped, and lets the record speak.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Terah; in sacred history he is the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran, an idolater of Ur who removed to Haran and died there.

expand to see more

TERAH, n. The son of Nahor, and the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran.

He dwelt in Ur of the Chaldees, and served other gods, as Joshua testifies.

He took his family and departed from Ur, intending to go into the land of Canaan.

Coming to Haran, he dwelt there, and did not proceed further.

He died in Haran, being two hundred and five years old.

Key Scripture

Gen 11:26 — "And Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran."

Gen 11:31 — "And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram's wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there."

Gen 11:32 — "And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran."

Jos 24:2 — "And Joshua said unto all the people, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods."

Modern Corruption

Abraham's ancestry is sanitized into a monotheistic heritage he inherited, when Scripture says his father served other gods — and the sanitizing quietly turns free election into family tradition.

expand to see more

A widespread popular telling makes Abraham the heir of a purer faith, or the lone monotheist in an idolatrous age who reasoned his way to the true God. Joshua flatly contradicts the first: Terah served other gods. And Scripture nowhere credits Abram with discovering anything. The initiative is entirely on the other side — “The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran” (Act 7:2). Sovereign grace reached into an idolater's household and took a man out of it. That is the doctrine the passage exists to teach, and every retelling that gives Abram a head start destroys it. Israel is told this at the covenant renewal precisely so that the nation will never think itself chosen for its pedigree.

The second corruption is a sentimentality that turns Terah into a hero for starting. He did start, and the text gives him that credit without comment. But it also records where he stopped, and Haran is not Canaan. There is a manner of religion that leaves the old country without ever arriving at the promise — out of Ur, short of the land, settled in a place with the family name on it and the old gods within reach. Scripture's word for the alternative is endurance: “we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end” (Heb 3:14). Terah is not condemned in the record. He is simply left in Haran, and the story goes on without him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Terach (H8646), Terah; 'Ur (H218), Ur; Charan (H2771), Haran; yashab (H3427), to dwell, settle; 'elohim 'acherim, other gods.

expand to see more

Hebrew Terach (H8646) — Terah; father of Abram, Nahor and Haran.

Hebrew 'Ur (H218) — Ur of the Chaldees, the city he left.

Hebrew Charan (H2771) — Haran, the city he stopped in and died in.

Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, remain, dwell, settle; the verb of Gen 11:31's last clause.

Hebrew 'acher (H312) — other, another; in the phrase “other gods” of Jos 24:2.

Usage

"“They served other gods” — the household grace reached into."

"“To go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there” — the whole tragedy in one verse."

"“Terah died in Haran” — halfway, and comfortable."
